title: Retention time calibration for RP-HPLC at pH 9
projectDescription: The change in pH of the mobile phase drastically changes the retention mechanism of peptides, rendering currently available retention time prediction models useless. The aim of this study is to create a dataset of peptide retention times under basic (pH 9) HPLC conditions, allowing for the creation of a retention time prediction model specific for these conditions. Peptides were separated using basic mobile phases and analyzed in positive ion mode, allowing identification with common shotgun proteomics pipeline.
sampleProcessingProtocol: HeLa cells (≈10^6 cells) were suspended in 400 μL of lysis buffer (1% w/w SDC, 10 mM TCEP, 20 mM CAA, and 100 mM TEAB buffer; pH 8), and cells were incubated in a shaker at 300 rpm at 90 °C for 30 min. Cells were lysed using an ultrasonic homogenizer (QSonica) for 4 min with 40% amplitude on ice, with 1 s on/off pulses. Before digestion, an 80 μL aliquot was diluted with 120 μL of TEAB buffer, 100 mM, pH 8. Trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) and GluC (Roche, Mannheim, Germany) were added at a ratio of 1:50 w/w and incubated for 4 h, at 25 °C (GluC) and 37 °C (trypsin). After that, a booster of each enzyme at a ratio of 1:100 w/w was added to the corresponding digest, and digestion was performed overnight. Three experiments were performed. (Experiment 1, July) An aliquot (15 μg) of the trypsin and GluC HeLa digest was loaded onto an Acquity UPLC M-Class CS C18 column (Waters, Etten-Leur, Netherlands) for offline reversed-phase low-pH fractionation using a Dionex Ultimate 3000 HPLC system (Thermo Scientific, Bremen, Germany). Peptides were loaded using buffer A (0.1% FA in water) and separated by increasing concentrations of buffer B (95% ACN and 0.1% FA in water) from 2 to 40% B in 70 min and from 40 to 95% B in 5 min. After 10 min at 95% B, the mobile phase composition was switched back to 2% B in 1 min and was held at 2% B for 4 min. Peptides were collected in 30 concatenated fractions in 10 different wells, using 3 min per eluting fraction. Collected fractions were dried in SpeedVac before LC-MS. (Experiment 2, March) Pierce HeLa digest (P/N 88328) was used as one of the samples, and all samples were analyzed in quadruplicate without fractionation. (Experiment 3, April) Only self-made protein digests were analyzed in triplicate without fractionation. LC-MS analysis was the same for all experiments. Peptides were dissolved in mobile phase A and 1 μg was injected into an UltiMate 3000 LC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germering, Germany) operating in high-pH RP-HPLC mode (mobile phases: 2.5 mM imidazole and 3% IPA in water (A); 2.5 mM imidazole and 3% IPA in 95% acetonitrile(B)) equipped with a self-packed analytical column (XBridge Premier Peptide BEH C18, 2.5 μm, 75 μm i.d., 18 cm length, 130 Å; Waters, Milford, MA, USA). The analytical gradient was from 2% to 40% B over 120 minutes with a flow rate of 250 nL/min, followed by washing the column at 95% B. Orbitrap Fusion Lumos (Thermo Scientific, San Jose, CA, USA) was operated in positive ion DDA mode. MS1 scans were acquired in Orbitrap (resolution: 120,000; scan range: 350 – 1500; maximum injection time: 200 ms; AGC target: 1e6). Precursors with charges from 1 to 4 (inclusive) with a minimum intensity of 2.5e4 were selected with an isolation window of 1.2 Th and fragmented by HCD with NCE of 36. Fragmented precursors were excluded for 20 seconds. MS2 scans were acquired in Orbitrap (resolution: 60,000, maximum injection time: 200 ms; AGC target: 1e5).
dataProcessingProtocol: Mass spectrometric data were converted to mzML format by ThermoRawFileParser (1.3.4) and searched with MSGF+ (v2022.01.07) against Uniprot human proteome (20185 proteins) supplemented with reversed decoys. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was used as the fixed modification, and oxidation of methionine and acetylation of protein N-terminus as variable modifications. Up to 2 or 4 missed cleavages were allowed for tryptic and Glu-C digests, respectively. Precursor mass tolerance was set to 10 ppm, and fragment mass tolerance was selected by the search engine. The results were rescored by Percolator (3.05). LC-MS elution profiles were calculated by Biosaur2, and confident peptide-spectrum matches (q-value < 0.01) were mapped to the LC-MS features by accurate monoisotopic m/z (5 ppm tolerance), retention time, and charge. The apex retention time of the LC-MS feature was used as the experimental retention time of the corresponding peptide. Average elution time was used for peptides detected more than once, while peptides with a retention time coefficient of variation above 0.1 were excluded.
